<reason>Both sides were skilled and format-compliant, but A built the more complete path. A's Rebuttal 1 decisively turned B's century-of-dubbing analogy (traditional dubbing used a different, paid human; AI synthesizes the performer's own vocal signature — "a forger can be extremely faithful"), and B's reply (the contract supplies authorization) assumed the very validity of boilerplate the motion contests. On B's strongest point — that opt-in just moves coercion to the audition — A gave a concrete, four-part answer (priced vs. zero-price, visible/regulable vs. invisible, clear entitlement vs. unconscionability lottery, and consent as the baseline that makes the bargaining B praises possible). B's counter ("page 34 with a date," signatures don't self-enforce) was punchy but only half-answered the priced-sale distinction. Meanwhile A's Q2 exposed a gap B never closed: publicity law and unfair-terms doctrine are the ex post lawsuit lottery A decried, and guild floors plausibly don't reach non-union extras or overseas dubbing artists. A conceded B's cost point honestly and reframed it as rightly allocated risk; B's closing mostly reasserted rather than re-engaged A's scoped-grant distinction. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1: flipping B's dubbing tradition ("a different human being — hired, paid, credited") plus the forger line gutted B's "not a new performance" core, and A4.2's catch that B2.3 reduces the "silenced audiences" objection to a margin claim further narrowed B's route.</best_rebuttal>
